name: Mecca (the Ka'ba)
description: The birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) around the Year of the Elephant, and the city where he spent the first fifty-three years of his life. Here he received the earliest revelations, preached in secret and then openly, endured the boycott of Banu Hashim, and lost both Khadijah and Abu Talib in a single year. The Ka'ba stood at the center of it all, and the Prophet returned to cleanse it of idols when Mecca was opened peacefully in Ramadan of 8 AH.
source_citation: Ibn Hisham, al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah, sections on the Prophet's birth and the Conquest of Mecca; Martin Lings, Muhammad, chapters 'The Year of the Elephant' and 'The Conquest of Mecca'
coord_note: Coordinates are the Ka'ba itself. Confident. Shown as a permanent map label, so excluded from the answer pool.

name: Cave of Hira (Jabal al-Nour)
era: 610 CE, roughly 13 years before the Hijrah
description: A small cave near the summit of a mountain a few kilometers northeast of Mecca. The Prophet had taken to retreating here for days at a time in worship and reflection. During one such retreat in the month of Ramadan, the angel Jibril came to him and pressed him three times, commanding him to recite. The first verses of Surat al-'Alaq were revealed, and he returned home trembling to Khadijah, asking to be wrapped in a cloak.
source_citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Beginning of Revelation, hadith of 'A'ishah (no. 3); Ibn Hisham, section on the beginning of prophethood; Lings, Muhammad, chapter 'The First Revelations'
coord_note: Coordinates are the mountain summit area. Confident.

name: Cave of Thawr (the Hijrah cave)
description: A cave on a mountain south of Mecca where the Prophet and Abu Bakr hid for three nights after slipping out of the city during the Hijrah. The Quraysh had posted a reward for their capture and their trackers came as far as the mouth of the cave. Abu Bakr feared they were finished; the Prophet replied that they were two with Allah as the third. Abu Bakr's son 'Abdullah brought news each evening and his daughter Asma' brought food, and their freed man 'Amir ibn Fuhayrah grazed his flock nearby to cover the tracks.
source_citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Merits of the Companions, the Hijrah narrative of 'A'ishah (no. 3905); Qur'an 9:40; Ibn Hisham, section on the Hijrah; Lings, Muhammad, chapter 'The Hijrah'
coord_note: Coordinates are the peak of Jabal Thawr. The cave is near the summit. Confident on the mountain, verify the exact cave point.

name: Ta'if
era: 10th year of the mission (about 619 CE) and again 8 AH
description: A walled hill town of orchards and vineyards east of Mecca, home of the tribe of Thaqif. After the death of Abu Talib, the Prophet walked here seeking support, and was rejected by its chiefs, who set their slaves and children on him and drove him out with stones. Bleeding, he rested in an orchard outside the town and made the supplication complaining of his weakness to Allah. Years later, after the Conquest of Mecca and the battle of Hunayn, the Muslims besieged Ta'if for roughly twenty days before withdrawing; Thaqif accepted Islam of their own accord the following year.
source_citation: Ibn Hisham, sections on the journey to Ta'if and the Siege of Ta'if; Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith of 'A'ishah on the hardest day at the 'Aqabah (no. 3231); Lings, Muhammad, chapters 'Ta'if' and 'The Siege of Ta'if'
coord_note: City center. Confident.

name: Medina (Yathrib)
description: The oasis town of Yathrib, home of the Aws and Khazraj tribes, which welcomed the Prophet after the Hijrah and became known simply as al-Madinah, the City. His camel Qaswa' knelt on a drying-floor for dates belonging to two orphan boys, and the mosque and his own quarters were built there. The constitution binding the Muslims, the Ansar, and the Jewish tribes was drawn up here; the direction of prayer was changed toward Mecca here; and the Prophet died and was buried here in his wife 'A'ishah's chamber in 11 AH.
source_citation: Ibn Hisham, sections on the arrival at Medina and the building of the mosque; Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith on the Prophet's arrival and the building of the mosque (no. 428); Lings, Muhammad, chapters 'The Entry into Medina' and 'The Succession and the Burial'
coord_note: Coordinates are the Prophet's Mosque. Confident. Shown as a permanent map label, so excluded from the answer pool.

name: Badr
description: A small settlement with wells on the caravan route between Mecca and Syria, about 130 km southwest of Medina. The Prophet set out with roughly three hundred men intending to intercept a Quraysh caravan led by Abu Sufyan, but the caravan escaped and a Meccan army of about a thousand came out instead. The Muslims reached the wells first and took them. The night before the battle rain fell, firming the sand on the Muslim side, and the Prophet spent the night in prayer. The Meccans were routed; Abu Jahl and many of the Quraysh chiefs were killed, and the victory was described in the Qur'an as a day on which the angels fought alongside the believers.
source_citation: Qur'an 3:123, 8:9-12; Ibn Hisham, section on the Great Battle of Badr; Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Military Expeditions, chapter on Badr; Lings, Muhammad, chapters 'The March to Badr' and 'The Battle of Badr'
coord_note: Modern town of Badr. The battlefield lies at the edge of the town. Confident to within a few km.

name: Mount Uhud
description: A long, reddish mountain immediately north of Medina, at whose foot the second great battle was fought. The Quraysh marched from Mecca with about three thousand men to avenge Badr. The Prophet placed fifty archers on a small hill to guard the army's flank and ordered them not to move whatever happened. The Muslims broke the Meccan line, but most of the archers left their post to join the plunder and Khalid ibn al-Walid's cavalry swept around behind them. The Prophet was wounded in the face and a false cry went up that he had been killed. Seventy Muslims fell, among them the Prophet's uncle Hamzah, and they lie buried at the foot of the mountain.
source_citation: Qur'an 3:121-180; Ibn Hisham, section on the Battle of Uhud; Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Military Expeditions, chapter on Uhud; Lings, Muhammad, chapters 'Uhud' and 'The Rout and the Return'
coord_note: Southern foot of the mountain near the martyrs' cemetery. The mountain itself is several km long, so this is a v1 whole-location pin. Verify.

name: Hudaybiyyah
description: A place with a well on the edge of the sacred precinct, west of Mecca on the road to Jeddah. The Prophet came with about fourteen hundred companions in pilgrim dress intending to perform 'umrah, and the Quraysh barred the way. His camel knelt here and refused to go on. After tense negotiations and a rumor that 'Uthman had been killed, the companions swore the Pledge of Ridwan under a tree to fight to the death. A ten-year truce was then agreed with Suhayl ibn 'Amr on terms that seemed humiliating to many of the companions, but which the Qur'an called a clear victory, and which opened the way for Islam to spread across Arabia.
source_citation: Qur'an 48:1-29; Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Conditions, the long hadith of al-Miswar ibn Makhramah and Marwan (no. 2731-2732); Ibn Hisham, section on the Expedition of al-Hudaybiyyah; Lings, Muhammad, chapter 'Hudaybiyah'
coord_note: Identified with the modern al-Shumaysi area west of Mecca. Coordinates are approximate and this one needs your verification most.

name: Khaybar
description: A cluster of fortified oases and date-palm plantations about 150 km north of Medina, inhabited by Jewish tribes who had allied with the enemies of Medina and helped assemble the coalition of the Trench. Shortly after Hudaybiyyah the Prophet marched here and took the forts one by one over several weeks. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib was given the standard and took the fort of al-Qamus. The inhabitants were allowed to remain and farm the land in return for half the harvest, and the spoils were distributed among those who had been present at Hudaybiyyah.
source_citation: Ibn Hisham, section on the Expedition of Khaybar; Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Military Expeditions, chapter on Khaybar; Sahih Muslim, Book of Virtues of the Companions, hadith of 'Ali receiving the standard; Lings, Muhammad, chapter 'Khaybar'
coord_note: Modern Khaybar town at the center of the oasis. Confident to within a few km.

name: Plain of Arafat
description: A wide plain about 20 km east of Mecca, bounded by low hills, where pilgrims gather on the ninth day of Dhul Hijjah. Here, during the Farewell Pilgrimage in the last year of his life, the Prophet delivered his sermon from his camel's back. He declared the sanctity of life and property, abolished the blood feuds and usury of the pre-Islamic period, commanded good treatment of women, and said he was leaving among them the Book of Allah. He asked whether he had delivered the message, and the crowd answered that he had. The verse announcing that the religion had been perfected was revealed at this standing.
source_citation: Qur'an 5:3; Sahih Muslim, Book of Pilgrimage, the long hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah describing the Prophet's Hajj (no. 1218); Ibn Hisham, section on the Farewell Pilgrimage; Lings, Muhammad, chapter 'The Farewell Pilgrimage'
coord_note: Coordinates are Jabal al-Rahmah, the hill on the plain. Confident.

name: Valley of Hunayn
description: A valley on the road from Mecca toward Ta'if where, a few weeks after the Conquest of Mecca, the tribes of Hawazin and Thaqif gathered to attack the Muslims. The Muslim army was the largest it had ever been, some twelve thousand, and some felt confident in their numbers. Archers hidden in the narrow valley ambushed them at dawn and the front ranks broke and fled. The Prophet stood firm with a small group and had al-'Abbas call out to the companions of the tree and the Ansar, and they rallied and turned the battle. The Qur'an mentions both the pride in numbers and the tranquility Allah then sent down.
source_citation: Qur'an 9:25-26; Ibn Hisham, section on the Battle of Hunayn; Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Military Expeditions, chapter on Hunayn; Sahih Muslim, hadith of al-'Abbas describing the rally; Lings, Muhammad, chapter 'Hunayn and Autas'
coord_note: Exact site is disputed. This pin follows the common identification with Wadi Hunayn near al-Shara'i east of Mecca. Approximate; cite one opinion per the v1 rule. Verify.

name: Tabuk
description: An oasis in the far north of the Hijaz, more than 600 km from Medina on the road to Syria. Hearing reports that the Byzantines were assembling forces, the Prophet called for a general mobilization in the heat of summer, at a time of drought and ripening harvest. This was the only expedition where he told the people plainly where they were going. About thirty thousand marched; some stayed behind with excuses, and the Qur'an later dealt at length with them. No Byzantine army appeared. The Prophet remained at Tabuk for some twenty days, concluding treaties with the local Christian and Jewish communities, and returned to Medina.
source_citation: Qur'an 9:38-59, 9:117-118; Ibn Hisham, section on the Expedition of Tabuk; Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Military Expeditions, the hadith of Ka'b ibn Malik on staying behind (no. 4418); Lings, Muhammad, chapter 'Tabuk'
coord_note: Modern city of Tabuk. Confident.

name: Al-Hijr (Mada'in Salih)
era: Rajab, 9 AH (630 CE), on the road to Tabuk
description: The ruined city of the people of Thamud, with tombs carved into the sandstone cliffs, which the army passed on the way north to Tabuk. The Prophet told the companions not to enter the dwellings of those who had been punished except weeping, lest what struck them should strike you too. He ordered that no one drink from its wells or use the water for cooking, and that any dough kneaded with it be fed to the camels, and he covered his head and quickened his camel until he had passed through the valley.
source_citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Prayer, hadith of Ibn 'Umar on passing al-Hijr (no. 433) and Book of Prophets (no. 3379-3381); Sahih Muslim, Book of Asceticism, hadith on al-Hijr (no. 2980-2981); Qur'an 7:73-79 on Thamud
coord_note: UNESCO site coordinates. Confident.

name: Quba Mosque
description: A settlement on the southern approach to Yathrib where the Prophet stopped before entering the city, staying several days among the Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf. He laid the foundation of the first mosque built in Islam here. Afterwards he made a habit of going out to it every Saturday, walking or riding, to pray two rak'ahs. The Qur'an speaks of a mosque founded on piety from the first day as more deserving that one should stand in it.
source_citation: Qur'an 9:108; Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Virtues of Medina, hadith of Ibn 'Umar on going to Quba every Saturday; Ibn Hisham, section on the Hijrah and the arrival at Quba; Lings, Muhammad, chapter 'The Entry into Medina'
coord_note: Modern mosque on the traditional site, south of Medina. Confident.

name: Masjid al-Qiblatayn
description: The mosque of the two qiblas, in the quarter of the Banu Salimah northwest of Medina. For about sixteen months after the Hijrah the Muslims prayed facing Jerusalem. The command to turn toward the Sacred Mosque in Mecca came down in the middle of a prayer, and the congregation turned where they stood, the men moving into the women's places and the women into the men's.
source_citation: Qur'an 2:142-150; Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Prayer, hadith of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib on the change of the qiblah; Sahih Muslim, Book of Mosques; Ibn Hisham, section on the change of the qiblah
coord_note: Modern mosque on the traditional site. Confident.

name: The Trench at Mount Sal'
description: A confederate army of some ten thousand marched on Medina. On the advice of Salman al-Farisi the Muslims dug a trench across the exposed northern approach, the city being shielded on its other sides by lava fields and dense palm groves. The defenders camped with Mount Sal' at their backs. The siege lasted about a month in cold and hunger, the Banu Qurayza broke their pact from within the city, and it ended when a bitter wind tore the besiegers' camp apart and they withdrew without a general battle.
source_citation: Qur'an 33:9-27; Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Military Expeditions, chapters on the Battle of the Trench; Sahih Muslim, Book of Jihad; Ibn Hisham, section on the Battle of the Ditch; Lings, Muhammad, chapter 'The Trench'
coord_note: Pinned at Mount Sal' in northwest Medina. The trench itself ran for some distance across the northern approach, so this is a point standing in for a line.

name: Jannat al-Baqi'
description: The burial ground of Medina, immediately southeast of the Prophet's Mosque. 'Uthman ibn Maz'un was the first of the Muhajirun buried here, and the Prophet's infant son Ibrahim was laid here. Many of the Companions and of the Prophet's household were buried in it over the following years. He used to come out to it at night and pray for those buried there.
source_citation: Sahih Muslim, Book of Funerals, hadith of 'A'ishah on the Prophet going out to al-Baqi' at night; Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Funerals; Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, on the burials at al-Baqi'
coord_note: Adjacent to the Prophet's Mosque. Confident. Sits close to the Medina pin, so both can appear in the same day's round.

name: Mina
era: The pledges at al-'Aqabah (620-622 CE) and the Farewell Pilgrimage, 10 AH (632 CE)
description: A valley east of Mecca on the pilgrimage route. At al-'Aqabah on its edge the Prophet met delegations from Yathrib in successive years and took the pledges that opened the way to the Hijrah. During the Farewell Pilgrimage he stayed here, stoned the pillars, offered the sacrifice, and addressed the people on the Day of Sacrifice.
source_citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Hajj, chapters on Mina and the Day of Sacrifice; Sahih Muslim, Book of Hajj, the long hadith of Jabir on the Farewell Pilgrimage; Ibn Hisham, sections on the first and second pledges of al-'Aqabah
coord_note: Valley centre near the Jamarat. Confident.

name: Muzdalifah
description: The open ground between Arafat and Mina where pilgrims halt for the night after the standing at Arafat. On the Farewell Pilgrimage the Prophet prayed the sunset and night prayers together here, slept until dawn, then stood at al-Mash'ar al-Haram in supplication until the light was full before moving on to Mina.
source_citation: Qur'an 2:198 on al-Mash'ar al-Haram; Sahih Muslim, Book of Hajj, the hadith of Jabir on the Farewell Pilgrimage; Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Hajj, chapters on Muzdalifah
coord_note: Centre of the plain, between Arafat and Mina. Confident.

name: Al-Ji'ranah
description: A valley northeast of Mecca where the Prophet halted after Hunayn and the siege of Ta'if to divide the captives and the spoils. He gave generously to Quraysh chiefs newly reconciled to Islam, which stung the Ansar until he gathered them and asked whether they would rather go home with sheep and camels or with the Messenger of God. He entered ihram here for 'umrah, and it remains a miqat for those in Mecca.
source_citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Military Expeditions, chapters on Hunayn and the division of the spoils; Sahih Muslim, Book of Zakat, the hadith of the Ansar and the spoils of Hunayn; Ibn Hisham, section on the division at al-Ji'ranah
coord_note: Approximate. Northeast of Mecca on the road toward Ta'if. Needs verification.

name: Dhul Hulayfah (Abyar 'Ali)
description: A valley some nine kilometres southwest of Medina where the Prophet entered ihram when setting out for 'umrah and again for the Farewell Pilgrimage, and which he fixed as the miqat for the people of Medina. He prayed here and passed the night before travelling on toward Mecca.
source_citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Hajj, chapters on the mawaqit and on Dhul Hulayfah; Sahih Muslim, Book of Hajj, hadith of Ibn 'Umar on the mawaqit
coord_note: Site of the modern Abyar 'Ali mosque. Confident.

name: Al-Masjid al-Aqsa (Bayt al-Maqdis)
era: Rajab, about a year before the Hijrah (around 621 CE)
description: The far mosque of the Night Journey. The Prophet was carried by night from the Sacred Mosque in Mecca to this sanctuary, led the prophets in prayer there, and was raised through the heavens, returning before morning. The five daily prayers were prescribed during that night. Jerusalem was also the first qiblah, toward which the Muslims prayed for about sixteen months after the Hijrah.
source_citation: Qur'an 17:1 and 53:1-18; Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Virtues of the Ansar, chapters on the Night Journey and the Ascension; Sahih Muslim, Book of Faith, the hadith of the Isra'; Ibn Hisham, section on the Night Journey
coord_note: Al-Aqsa compound, Jerusalem. Confident on position. Far outside the Hijaz - see the scoring note in the README. Shown as a permanent map label, so excluded from the answer pool.

name: Abyssinia (Aksum)
description: The Christian kingdom across the Red Sea to which the Prophet sent the persecuted believers, saying that its king was one under whom no one is wronged. Two groups migrated there. When Quraysh sent envoys demanding their return, Ja'far ibn Abi Talib spoke before the Negus and recited the opening of Surah Maryam on Jesus and his mother, and the Negus wept and refused to surrender them.
source_citation: Ibn Hisham, section on the migration to Abyssinia and the speech of Ja'far before the Negus; Qur'an 19:16-33 as recited there; Musnad Ahmad, hadith of Umm Salamah on the Abyssinian migration; Lings, Muhammad, chapter 'The Abyssinian Migration'
coord_note: Pinned at Aksum, the kingdom's capital. The migrants' exact place of settlement is not fixed in the sources. Far outside the Hijaz.

name: Mu'tah
description: A village in the Balqa' district south of modern Amman where a force of three thousand met a far larger Byzantine and allied Arab army. The Prophet had named three commanders in succession: Zayd ibn Harithah fell, then Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, then 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah. Khalid ibn al-Walid then took up the banner and withdrew the army intact. The Prophet announced the deaths in Medina on the day they happened.
source_citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Military Expeditions, chapter on the Battle of Mu'tah and the hadith of the three commanders; Ibn Hisham, section on the expedition to Mu'tah; Lings, Muhammad, chapter 'Mutah'
coord_note: Modern Mu'tah, Jordan, near Karak. Outside the Hijaz.

name: Dumat al-Jandal
description: An oasis and fortress town at the northern end of the Wadi Sirhan, on the caravan route toward Syria. The Prophet led an expedition toward it in 5 AH. After Tabuk he sent Khalid ibn al-Walid, who captured its ruler Ukaydir ibn 'Abd al-Malik while he was out hunting by night and brought him to Medina, where terms were agreed.
source_citation: Ibn Hisham, sections on the expedition to Dumat al-Jandal and on Khalid's raid after Tabuk; Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, on the capture of Ukaydir; al-Waqidi, Kitab al-Maghazi
coord_note: Historic site at modern Al-Jawf, near Sakaka. Confident.

name: Tayma
era: 9 AH (630 CE), in the aftermath of Tabuk
description: An ancient walled oasis with a famous well on the northern caravan road, long settled by Jewish tribes and known to pre-Islamic poets. It came to terms and agreed to pay the jizyah in the aftermath of the Tabuk expedition, bringing the northern oases within the new order without fighting.
source_citation: Ibn Hisham and al-Waqidi, sections on the Tabuk expedition and the northern oases; Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, on the agreements with Tayma' and the northern settlements
coord_note: Oasis town centre. Confident on the town. Its role is recorded briefly and in less detail than the battles.

name: Ayla (Aqaba)
description: The port at the head of the gulf, where the Syrian and Egyptian roads meet. While the army lay at Tabuk its Christian ruler Yuhannah ibn Ru'bah came out, made peace, and agreed to pay the jizyah. The Prophet wrote him a guarantee of protection and gave him a cloak: one of the earliest treaties made with a non-Muslim frontier town.
source_citation: Ibn Hisham, section on the Tabuk expedition and the treaty with Yuhannah ibn Ru'bah of Aylah; al-Waqidi, Kitab al-Maghazi; Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat
coord_note: Ancient Ayla lies within modern Aqaba, Jordan. Outside the Hijaz.

name: Jeddah
description: The Red Sea port serving Mecca, about seventy kilometres west of the sanctuary. It was from this stretch of coast that the first migrants took ship for Abyssinia, and it remained the sea gate through which pilgrims and trade reached the holy city. The caliph 'Uthman later made it the official port of Mecca.
source_citation: Ibn Hisham, section on the migration to Abyssinia and the embarkation on the Red Sea coast; al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan, on the establishment of Jeddah as the port of Mecca
coord_note: Modern city centre / historic Al-Balad. Confident on the port. The exact embarkation point for Abyssinia is not fixed; some reports name al-Shu'aybah instead. Shown as a permanent map label, so excluded from the answer pool.

name: Yanbu al-Bahr
description: A coastal settlement of abundant springs on the Red Sea, northwest of Medina. The earliest expeditions sent to intercept Quraysh caravans on the coastal road operated in this district, including the march to al-'Ushayrah in its hinterland, in the months before Badr.
source_citation: Ibn Hisham, sections on the early expeditions and the march to al-'Ushayrah; al-Waqidi, Kitab al-Maghazi, on the coastal expeditions before Badr
coord_note: Modern port city. The early expeditions ranged across this district rather than one fixed point, so the pin stands for a region.

name: Al-Juhfah
era: Prophetic era, fixed as a miqat
description: A settlement on the coastal road near modern Rabigh which the Prophet fixed as the point of entering ihram for pilgrims coming from Syria and Egypt. A hadith records his prayer that the fever then afflicting Medina be moved to al-Juhfah, which was at that time an unhealthy place.
source_citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Hajj, chapter on the mawaqit; Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Virtues of Medina, hadith of 'A'ishah on the prayer concerning the fever of Medina; Sahih Muslim, Book of Hajj, hadith of Ibn 'Abbas on the mawaqit
coord_note: Site near modern Rabigh. The old settlement is ruined and its exact position is debated. Approximate.

name: 'Usfan
description: A staging post on the road between Mecca and Medina, some eighty kilometres north of Mecca. The Prophet camped here on the march toward Hudaybiyyah when he learned that Khalid ibn al-Walid, then still fighting for Quraysh, was watching the road ahead with cavalry, and he turned aside by a rough track to the right. The prayer of fear is also reported to have been prayed at this place.
source_citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Military Expeditions, chapter on the expedition of al-Hudaybiyyah; Sunan Abi Dawud and Sunan al-Nasa'i, chapters on the prayer of fear at 'Usfan; Ibn Hisham, section on the march to al-Hudaybiyyah
coord_note: Modern 'Usfan on the Mecca-Medina road. Reasonably confident.

name: Al-Abwa'
era: About 6 BH (576 CE) and 2 AH (623 CE)
description: A village on the road between Mecca and Medina where the Prophet's mother Aminah died as she returned from visiting her family in Yathrib, leaving him orphaned at about six years old. Years later the first expedition he led in person, known as the raid of al-Abwa' or Waddan, went out to this district.
source_citation: Ibn Hisham, sections on the death of Aminah at al-Abwa' and on the expedition of Waddan; Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat; Sahih Muslim, Book of Funerals, hadith on the Prophet visiting his mother's grave
coord_note: Approximate. The village lies between Mecca and Medina toward Rabigh; the sources place it by stages along the road rather than by fixed position. Needs verification.

name: Fadak
description: A fertile oasis of date palms and springs north of Medina, not far from Khaybar. After Khaybar fell its inhabitants sued for terms without a battle, agreeing to surrender half their produce. Because it was taken without fighting it was treated as fay' at the Prophet's disposal rather than as spoils to be divided among an army, and its status was disputed after his death.
source_citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Military Expeditions, chapter on Khaybar; Qur'an 59:6-7 on fay'; Ibn Hisham, section on Khaybar and Fadak; al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan
coord_note: Commonly identified with modern al-Ha'it in Ha'il province. Approximate; needs verification.

name: Najran
description: An oasis region in the far south with a long-established Christian community. Its bishops and chiefs came to Medina as a delegation, debated the nature of Jesus with the Prophet in his mosque, and were invited to a mutual imprecation. They declined it, made a treaty securing their churches and property in exchange for tribute, and returned home.
source_citation: Qur'an 3:59-63, the verse of mubahalah; Ibn Hisham, section on the delegation of Najran; Sahih Muslim, Book of the Virtues of the Companions, hadith on the mubahalah; Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, on the delegations
coord_note: Modern Najran, far southern Saudi Arabia near the Yemeni border. Well outside the Hijaz.

name: Bosra (Busra al-Sham)
era: The Prophet's youth (about 582 CE) and 8 AH (629 CE)
description: A Byzantine caravan city in southern Syria and the usual northern terminus of the Meccan trade route. The Prophet is reported to have travelled here as a boy with his uncle Abu Talib, where the monk Bahira noticed signs of prophethood in him and warned Abu Talib to guard him carefully. Later the killing of the Prophet's envoy on the way to its governor was among the causes of the expedition to Mu'tah.
source_citation: Ibn Hisham, section on the journey to Syria and the monk Bahira; al-Tirmidhi, Book of Virtues, on the story of Bahira; Ibn Hisham, section on the causes of Mu'tah
coord_note: Ancient city in Daraa province, Syria. Outside the Hijaz. Note that the Bahira episode rests mainly on the sira literature and is weaker in the hadith collections.

name: Wadi Nakhlah
description: A valley on the road between Mecca and Ta'if. The Prophet stopped here on the way back from Ta'if, and while he prayed at night a company of jinn listened to the Qur'an and believed. The first expedition in which blood was shed also took place in this valley, when a small party under 'Abdullah ibn Jahsh attacked a Quraysh caravan during a sacred month, raising the question the Qur'an then answered about fighting in the sacred months.
source_citation: Qur'an 72:1-19 and 46:29-32 on the jinn; Qur'an 2:217 on fighting in the sacred month; Ibn Hisham, sections on the return from Ta'if and the expedition of 'Abdullah ibn Jahsh; Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Tafsir, on Surah al-Jinn
coord_note: Approximate. Wadi Nakhlah lies east of Mecca toward Ta'if and the sources differ on the exact spot. Needs verification.
